exhibits.title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine
exhibits.publicStory: Menabrea's sketch of Babbage's Analytical Engine, translated with notes by Ada Lovelace, appeared in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs in 1843. Note G works through a table for the Bernoulli numbers.
exhibits.editorialNote: Gutenberg and the Wikisource sketch page are transcriptions. The Internet Archive item is a scan of Scientific Memoirs volume III (1843), where the sketch begins on page 666 and Note G gives the Bernoulli table. The separate Wikisource Notes subpage returned 404, so it is not cited.

figure.alt: Note G diagram titled Diagram for the computation by the Engine of the Numbers of Bernoulli.
figure.credit: Public-domain scan of the Bernoulli diagram. Wikimedia Commons file page states Public Domain Mark 1.0.

fieldChange.before: A calculating engine was discussed as a machine for tables, without a published general procedure written for it.
fieldChange.after: The 1843 translation of Menabrea's sketch, with Lovelace's Note G, works through a table for the Bernoulli numbers on the Analytical Engine.

exhibits.title: The Laws of Thought
exhibits.publicStory: The opened title page reads An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, on which are founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probabilities, by George Boole, London: Walton and Maberly, Cambridge: Macmillan and Co., 1854.
exhibits.editorialNote: The shipped scan is Internet Archive item aninvestigation00boolgoog, whose metadata says not in copyright in the US.

figure.alt: Title page reading An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, by George Boole, London, Walton and Maberly, 1854.
figure.credit: Title page of the 1854 edition. Public-domain scan from the Internet Archive.

fieldChange.before: Logic was taught as a verbal art, apart from the manipulation of algebraic equations.
fieldChange.after: The opened 1854 title page presents Boole's book as an investigation of the laws of thought on which the mathematical theories of logic and probabilities are founded.

exhibits.title: On Computable Numbers
exhibits.publicStory: A. M. Turing's On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem, appeared in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, series 2, volume 42.
exhibits.editorialNote: The opened Crossref record dates the print issue 1937. It does not give a received-in-1936 date. This room keeps 1936 as the working year.

figure.alt: A state table with rows q1 and q2 and columns for symbols 0 and 1.
figure.credit: Original state-table diagram, redrawn after the London Mathematical Society paper. The opened record dates the print issue 1937. Not a scan.

fieldChange.before: The Entscheidungsproblem asked whether a definite method could decide every statement of a formal system, without a published account of what such a method was.
fieldChange.after: Turing's paper in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society defines computable numbers by a machine and applies that definition to the Entscheidungsproblem.

exhibits.title: Relay and switching circuits
exhibits.publicStory: Claude Shannon's A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits appeared in the Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, volume 57, pages 713–723, in 1938.
exhibits.editorialNote: The DOI record was opened. The IEEE Xplore HTML was a bot challenge and was not read.

figure.alt: Two relay boxes in series with a lamp.
figure.credit: Original relay diagram for this room. Not a copy of a figure from the 1938 paper.

fieldChange.before: Relay circuits were drawn as electrical arrangements, and symbolic logic was a separate study.
fieldChange.after: Shannon's 1938 paper gives a symbolic analysis of relay and switching circuits, in the Transactions of the AIEE, volume 57, pages 713–723.

exhibits.title: McCulloch–Pitts neuron
exhibits.publicStory: McCulloch and Pitts published a calculus that treats all-or-none neural events with propositional logic and pairs logical expressions with nets.

figure.alt: Two input circles joined by lines to one output circle.
figure.credit: Original net diagram, redrawn after the 1943 paper. Not a copy of a journal figure.

exhibits.technicalAccount: The 1943 paper in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics states that the all-or-none character of nervous activity lets neural events be treated by propositional logic. A net without circles has a description in that logic, and a logical expression meeting their conditions has a net that behaves as the expression describes. Nets with circles need further logical means.

fieldChange.before: A neuron was described physiologically, and propositional logic was a separate calculus.
fieldChange.after: The 1943 paper treats all-or-none neural events with propositional logic and pairs a logical expression with a net that behaves as that expression describes.

exhibits.title: Cybernetics
exhibits.publicStory: A 1948 edition is catalogued as Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics; or, Control and communication in the animal and the machine, from The Technology Press. The Internet Archive scan cited here is the 1961 second edition from MIT Press, not the 1948 printing.
exhibits.editorialNote: Open Library's edition record was opened. A title page was not. The record does not name Hermann et Cie.

figure.alt: A box labeled effector with a return path from its output back to its input.
figure.credit: Original feedback diagram for this room. The catalog record has no figure to copy.

fieldChange.before: Control in machines and communication in animals were catalogued as separate subjects.
fieldChange.after: A 1948 edition is catalogued as Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics; or, Control and communication in the animal and the machine.

exhibits.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
exhibits.publicStory: Shannon's 1948 paper defines a communication system as information source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, and measures a choice among messages with a logarithm.

figure.alt: Five boxes in a row, labeled source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, with a noise mark above the channel.
figure.credit: Original diagram of the five parts named in the paper's text. Not a copy of the printed figure.

exhibits.technicalAccount: The paper's text names five parts of a communication system: information source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, and it places a noise source on the channel. A message is one selected from a set of possible messages. When that set is finite and choices are equally likely, the measure is a logarithm of the number of messages. The discrete noiseless case is developed before the continuous case.

fieldChange.before: Communication engineering had no shared measure for a choice among possible messages.
fieldChange.after: The 1948 paper names an information source, a transmitter, a channel, a receiver, and a destination, and it measures a finite set of equally likely messages by a logarithm of that number.

exhibits.title: Turing's imitation game
exhibits.publicStory: Alan Turing published Computing Machinery and Intelligence in Mind, proposing the Imitation Game as an operational stand-in for whether machines can think.

fieldChange.before: Asking whether a machine can think had no agreed operation that would settle the question.
fieldChange.after: Turing's 1950 paper in Mind proposes the imitation game as a stand-in for that question.

exhibits.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
exhibits.publicStory: A summer workshop at Dartmouth, proposed in August 1955 as a “2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence”; the proposal's title introduced the term. It is widely regarded as the field's founding event.

fieldChange.before: Research on machines and intelligence had no common name.
fieldChange.after: The 31 August 1955 proposal, A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, asks for a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence.

exhibits.title: Rosenblatt's Perceptron
exhibits.publicStory: Frank Rosenblatt published the Perceptron, a probabilistic model of a learning network.

fieldChange.before: A learning machine was a proposal, not a published model with a training rule.
fieldChange.after: Rosenblatt's 1958 paper presents the perceptron as a probabilistic model for storing and organizing information.

exhibits.title: DENDRAL
exhibits.publicStory: The DENDRAL project at Stanford identified chemical structures. Its builders' 1993 case study calls it the first expert system for scientific hypothesis formation.

fieldChange.before: A program that proposed a chemical structure from instrument data was a hope, not a recorded project.
fieldChange.after: The builders' 1993 case study calls DENDRAL the first expert system for scientific hypothesis formation. The Computer History Museum keeps the project's papers.

exhibits.title: ELIZA
exhibits.publicStory: Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA, a pattern-matching conversational program. Many users treated it as understanding them, a documented case of over-attribution later called the Eliza effect.

fieldChange.before: A program that answered in sentences was easy to treat as a program that understood the person typing.
fieldChange.after: Weizenbaum's 1966 paper describes ELIZA as keyword rules that transform a sentence, and he writes that the relation of appearance to reality stays with the playwright.

exhibits.title: ALPAC report
exhibits.publicStory: The Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee report found machine translation had not delivered, after which U.S. government MT funding was sharply reduced.

fieldChange.before: U.S. agencies were funding machine translation in the expectation of a working system.
fieldChange.after: The 1966 National Academies report, Language and Machines, is the committee's published finding that machine translation had not delivered what that funding assumed.

exhibits.title: Limits of the single-layer perceptron
exhibits.publicStory: Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons proved formal limits of single-layer networks, including XOR.
exhibits.editorialNote: The MIT Press DOI is the 2017 reissue of the book; its page returned 403 and was not read. Open Library catalogues the 1969 printing. The XOR limit is also stated on the Wikipedia book page.

fieldChange.before: A single layer of neuron-like units was treated as a route to any classification that mattered.
fieldChange.after: Minsky and Papert's book, cited here in the MIT Press 2017 reissue, states formal limits of a single-layer perceptron, including exclusive-or. Open Library catalogues the 1969 printing.

exhibits.title: Lighthill Report
exhibits.publicStory: The Lighthill Report to the UK Science Research Council concluded AI had failed to produce the promised major impact, and was followed by deep UK funding cuts.
exhibits.editorialNote: The report is dated July 1972 and was published in 1973. The funding cuts that followed are stated on the Wikipedia page, not in the report.

fieldChange.before: UK support for artificial intelligence assumed the work would produce the impact that had been promised.
fieldChange.after: Lighthill's survey, in the Edinburgh copy, says that in no part of the field had the discoveries produced the major impact that was then promised. The Chilton host did not answer, so it is not cited.

exhibits.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
exhibits.publicStory: IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov.

fieldChange.before: No chess computer had beaten a reigning world champion in a match under regular time controls.
fieldChange.after: IBM's history says Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997, after Kasparov had won their 1996 match.

exhibits.title: Watson wins Jeopardy!
exhibits.publicStory: IBM Watson won Jeopardy! against the champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings in February 2011.

fieldChange.before: A question-answering system had not beaten the strongest human champions of a televised quiz on the air.
fieldChange.after: IBM's history says Watson defeated Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings on Jeopardy! in February 2011.

exhibits.title: AlexNet at ILSVRC
exhibits.publicStory: AlexNet won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a GPU-trained convolutional network, with a top-5 error rate of 15.3 percent, against 26.2 percent for the second-best entry.

fieldChange.before: The next-best ImageNet entry in 2012 still relied on engineered features, with a top-5 error of 26.2 percent.
fieldChange.after: The NeurIPS 2012 paper reports that an average of convolutional networks reached 15.3 percent top-5 error on ILSVRC-2012.

exhibits.title: Generative adversarial networks
exhibits.publicStory: Goodfellow and colleagues introduced generative adversarial networks.

fieldChange.before: A generator of new samples was trained to match a data set, without a second network trained to tell real from generated.
fieldChange.after: The 2014 paper proposes two models trained together: a generator, and a discriminator that estimates whether a sample came from the training data.

exhibits.title: Tay
exhibits.publicStory: Microsoft took its Tay chatbot offline within a day of its March 2016 Twitter launch, after Tay posted what Microsoft called wildly inappropriate and reprehensible words and images.

fieldChange.before: A public chatbot was launched on the assumption that conversation on the open internet would stay inside the filters shipped with it.
fieldChange.after: Microsoft's 25 March 2016 post is the team's account of taking Tay offline. The incident report dates the offensive posts to about 16 hours after the Twitter launch.

exhibits.title: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
exhibits.publicStory: DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Go player Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul in March 2016. In game two it played Move 37, which DeepMind's account says upended centuries of traditional wisdom.

fieldChange.before: A published Go program had not yet played a match against a player of Lee Sedol's standing.
fieldChange.after: Nature's January 2016 paper is the account of the network-and-search program. DeepMind's own page is the record of the later match: a 4–1 win over Lee Sedol in Seoul in March 2016.

exhibits.title: Attention Is All You Need
exhibits.publicStory: Eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research (one listed at the University of Toronto, with work performed at Google) published Attention Is All You Need, introducing the Transformer. The paper reports 28.4 BLEU on WMT-2014 English–German and 41.8 BLEU on English–French after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs. Authors are credited as equal contributors.

fieldChange.before: The strongest translation models were recurrent or convolutional networks, with attention as a connection between an encoder and a decoder.
fieldChange.after: The paper proposes a network that uses attention alone, and it reports 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French after 3.5 days on eight GPUs.

exhibits.title: AlphaFold2
exhibits.publicStory: DeepMind's AlphaFold2 made highly accurate protein-structure prediction from amino-acid sequence possible, a long-standing structural-biology challenge.

fieldChange.before: A protein's folded shape was predicted from its sequence only approximately, and the hard targets at the structure contest were still mostly unsolved.
fieldChange.after: The result shown at CASP14 in 2020 was published in Nature in 2021. The paper reports highly accurate structure prediction from amino-acid sequence. The plaque keeps 2020 as the year of that contest.

exhibits.title: ChatGPT research preview
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free research preview on 30 November 2022.
exhibits.editorialNote: The 100 million users clause was removed. No news page stating that figure was opened. The OpenAI post is the 30 November 2022 announcement.

fieldChange.before: A large language model was available through an API and demos, not as a free conversational research preview.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's 30 November 2022 post introduces ChatGPT as a free research preview, trained to answer in dialogue.

exhibits.title: Statement on AI Risk
exhibits.publicStory: The Center for AI Safety's one-sentence statement on extinction-scale AI risk was signed by AI researchers and the heads of major labs. A survey of AI-conference authors, published in January 2024, found that between 38 and 51 percent of respondents gave at least a 10 percent chance to advanced AI leading to outcomes as bad as human extinction. That range is a survey statistic, not a consensus forecast.

fieldChange.before: Extinction-scale risk from AI was a topic of talks, without one short public statement from lab leaders and without a counted survey of conference authors.
fieldChange.after: The Center for AI Safety published a one-sentence statement on that risk. The survey paper, published in January 2024, says between 38 and 51 percent of respondents gave at least a 10 percent chance to advanced AI leading to outcomes as bad as human extinction.

exhibits.title: EU AI Act
exhibits.publicStory: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on 1 August 2024 as a horizontal AI law with a phased, risk-tiered timeline. The regulation sets fines of up to €35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of the Article 5 prohibitions.

fieldChange.before: Rules for AI systems in the European Union were national or sectoral, without one horizontal regulation in force.
fieldChange.after: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on EUR-Lex, sets a fine of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5. The plaque dates entry into force, not a later consolidated text.

exhibits.title: 2024 Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry
exhibits.publicStory: The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for work enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded half to David Baker for computational protein design, and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction.

fieldChange.before: The physics and chemistry prizes had not been given for the machine-learning work named here.
fieldChange.after: The Nobel Foundation's 2024 summaries award physics to John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for discoveries that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks, and chemistry half to David Baker for computational protein design and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences says Hassabis and Jumper developed AlphaFold2.

exhibits.title: BERT
exhibits.publicStory: Google's BERT pre-trained a Transformer on plain text, reading the words on both sides of each gap, then fine-tuned it to new state-of-the-art results on eleven language tasks. Google open-sourced it in November 2018, saying anyone could train a state-of-the-art question-answering system in about 30 minutes on a single Cloud TPU.

fieldChange.before: Pre-trained language models read text in one direction, or joined a left-to-right model with a right-to-left one.
fieldChange.after: The 2018 paper pre-trains a Transformer on the words to both sides at once, and reports new state-of-the-art results on eleven language tasks after fine-tuning.

exhibits.title: GPT-2
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-2, a 1.5-billion-parameter Transformer trained on millions of web pages, set state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language-modelling datasets without being trained for any of them. OpenAI released it in stages.
exhibits.editorialNote: Both sources are OpenAI's own; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains. The paper PDF is undated: 2019 rests on the GitHub repository and the Epoch AI date of 14 February 2019.

fieldChange.before: Language tasks were approached by training a model on a labelled data set for each task.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's paper reports that a 1.5-billion-parameter model trained on WebText, a data set of millions of web pages, set state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language-modelling data sets without training on them.

exhibits.title: GPT-3
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, which its paper calls 10 times more than any previous non-sparse language model. It performed many tasks from a few examples written as text, with no fine-tuning.

fieldChange.before: A language model needed a fine-tuning data set of thousands of labelled examples for each new task.
fieldChange.after: The 2020 paper reports that GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, performed many tasks from a few examples given as text, with no fine-tuning.

exhibits.title: Wu Dao 2.0
exhibits.publicStory: Wu Dao 2.0, with 1.75 trillion parameters, was released in June 2021, and its creators say that is ten times as many as GPT-3. Tsinghua University says it understands and generates text and images in Chinese, English and other mainstream languages, and that its development was led by Jie Tang, a Tsinghua professor and vice director of academics at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence.
exhibits.editorialNote: No page from the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence was found, so the story says only what Tsinghua's page says. That page is undated and says the model was released in June; Engadget's report of 2 June 2021 dates the year.

fieldChange.before: China's first super-scale natural-language model had been unveiled in early 2021.
fieldChange.after: Tsinghua's account says Wu Dao 2.0 was released in June with 1.75 trillion parameters, which its creators put at ten times GPT-3.

exhibits.title: Chinchilla
exhibits.publicStory: DeepMind found that large language models were undertrained, and that model size and training data should grow together. Its 70-billion-parameter Chinchilla used the same compute as the 280-billion-parameter Gopher with four times the data, and outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 and Megatron-Turing NLG on a large range of tasks.

fieldChange.before: Language models were being scaled up in size while the amount of training data stayed about the same.
fieldChange.after: The 2022 paper finds that model size and training tokens should be scaled equally. Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and four times Gopher's data for the same compute, outperforms Gopher.

exhibits.title: LLaMA
exhibits.publicStory: Meta released LLaMA in February 2023 in four sizes from 7 to 65 billion parameters, trained only on publicly available data, under a noncommercial research licence. Its paper reports that the 13-billion-parameter version outperforms the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

fieldChange.before: The strongest language models were trained in part on data sets that were not publicly available.
fieldChange.after: The 2023 paper trains models from 7 to 65 billion parameters on publicly available data alone, and reports that the 13-billion-parameter model outperforms GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

exhibits.title: GPT-4
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-4 accepts images and text and produces text, and its technical report says it passed a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers. The report also says OpenAI predicted parts of GPT-4's performance from models trained with no more than 1/1,000th of its compute.
exhibits.editorialNote: Both sources carry OpenAI's own document; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains.

fieldChange.before: OpenAI's earlier GPT-3.5 scored around the bottom 10% of test takers on a simulated bar exam.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's 2023 technical report says GPT-4, which accepts images and text, passed the simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers.

exhibits.title: Qwen
exhibits.publicStory: Alibaba Cloud released its Qwen language models openly on ModelScope and Hugging Face, starting with Qwen-7B on 3 August 2023. The series grew to base and chat models of 1.8, 7, 14 and 72 billion parameters.

fieldChange.before: Alibaba Cloud had not released the weights of its Qwen language models.
fieldChange.after: The QwenLM repository records the open release of Qwen-7B on ModelScope and Hugging Face on 3 August 2023, and base and chat models of 1.8, 7, 14 and 72 billion parameters.

exhibits.title: Falcon-180B
exhibits.publicStory: The Technology Innovation Institute's Falcon-180B has 180 billion parameters and was trained on over 3.5 trillion tokens, which its authors call the largest openly documented pretraining run. TII released it under a permissive licence, alongside 7B and 40B models.
exhibits.editorialNote: The model card gives no release date. The paper is from November 2023 and Epoch AI gives 6 September 2023.

fieldChange.before: No openly documented language-model pretraining run had used 3.5 trillion tokens.
fieldChange.after: The Falcon paper says Falcon-180B was trained on over 3.5 trillion tokens, the largest openly documented pretraining run. TII released it with 7B and 40B models under a permissive licence.

exhibits.title: Mistral 7B
exhibits.publicStory: Mistral AI, a French company headquartered in Paris, released Mistral 7B, a 7.3-billion-parameter model, on 27 September 2023 under the Apache 2.0 licence, so anyone could use it without restrictions. The company says it outperforms Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks.
exhibits.editorialNote: Neither Mistral source states the country; the Wikipedia article says the company is French and headquartered in Paris.

fieldChange.before: Llama 2 13B, with almost twice the parameters, was the open model Mistral 7B was measured against.
fieldChange.after: Mistral AI's 27 September 2023 announcement releases the 7.3-billion-parameter Mistral 7B under Apache 2.0 and says it outperforms Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks.

exhibits.title: OpenAI o1
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's o1 models are trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using a chain of thought, so they can produce a long chain of thought before they answer. OpenAI's system card, dated 5 December 2024, says o1 was previously called o1-preview.
exhibits.editorialNote: Both sources carry OpenAI's own document; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains. The arXiv copy was revised later; the story uses the original date.

fieldChange.before: OpenAI's chat models were not trained to produce a long chain of thought before answering.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's o1 system card, dated 5 December 2024, says the o1 models are trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought.

exhibits.title: DeepSeek-V3
exhibits.publicStory: DeepSeek-V3 is a mixture-of-experts model with 671 billion parameters, of which 37 billion are active for each token, pre-trained on 14.8 trillion tokens. Its report says full training took 2.788 million H800 GPU hours, and DeepSeek released the weights with commercial use allowed.

fieldChange.before: A dense language model uses all of its parameters for every token.
fieldChange.after: The DeepSeek-V3 report describes a mixture-of-experts model with 671 billion parameters, 37 billion active for each token, whose full training took 2.788 million H800 GPU hours.

exhibits.title: DeepSeek-R1
exhibits.publicStory: DeepSeek showed that a language model's reasoning could be improved through reinforcement learning alone, without human-written reasoning examples, and published the work in Nature in September 2025. DeepSeek released R1's weights under the MIT licence and says R1 performs comparably to OpenAI's o1 on maths, code and reasoning.
exhibits.editorialNote: Nature 645, 633–638 (2025). The arXiv copy was revised later; the story uses the original dates.

fieldChange.before: Reasoning in language models was improved by training on human-written reasoning examples.
fieldChange.after: The Nature paper reports that R1's reasoning was improved through reinforcement learning alone, without human-labelled reasoning examples.

exhibits.title: GPT-6 Astra
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra system card (3 September 2026) calls it the most capable model OpenAI has ever broadly deployed, and the first to reach the Critical level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework. Constellation Research reported that OpenAI launched it first to customers in its Daybreak program, before broad availability.
exhibits.editorialNote: The plaque states no hardware or GPU count: OpenAI's pages that could be opened do not name the hardware. Training compute is an Epoch AI estimate and appears only on the Globe.

fieldChange.before: No model OpenAI had deployed had reached the Critical level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework.
fieldChange.after: The 3 September 2026 system card says GPT-6 Astra is the first to reach that level. Constellation Research reports the same, calling Astra OpenAI's first launch with critical cybersecurity capability.

exhibits.title: Mechanical and logical precursors
exhibits.publicStory: Nilsson's history treats Aristotle's syllogism as important for its form, Boole's 1854 Laws of Thought as showing that some logical reasoning can be done by manipulating equations, and Babbage's engines as engineering clues in that quest.
exhibits.editorialNote: Framing plaque. Nilsson's pages say the print version is Cambridge University Press and ask readers not to cite this PDF. The URL is the file that was opened. Not a single technical result.

figure.credit: Original illustration of the years in this room. Not a plate from Nilsson.

fieldChange.before: A history of the field could open at the first meeting that used the name, and leave earlier logic and machinery outside it.
fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey places the form of the syllogism, Boole's 1854 equations, and Babbage's engines inside that history, as clues rather than as one technical result.

exhibits.title: First AI winter
exhibits.publicStory: Retrospectives treat 1974–1980 as the first AI winter, when inflated promises met computational and theoretical limits of symbolic AI.

fieldChange.before: The funding cuts after 1973 were separate decisions, not yet one named period.
fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey is one later history that places those years in a longer story. The name AI winter is the label on the Wikipedia page for 1974–1980, not a name from 1974 itself.

exhibits.title: Expert systems commercial boom
exhibits.publicStory: A 1985 government report estimated AI-related activity funded by government and industry at about $400 million that year. A separate 1985 note put sales of AI software and hardware at about $150 million a year.
exhibits.editorialNote: The billion-dollar sentence was not on an institutional page opened for this edit. The $400 million estimate is the 1985 Argonne report. The $150 million sales figure is a 1985 journal note.

fieldChange.before: Expert systems were laboratory programs, without a published government estimate of that year's spending.
fieldChange.after: The Argonne report opened on OSTI estimates AI-related activity, government and industry, at about $400 million in 1985.

exhibits.title: LISP-machine market collapse
exhibits.publicStory: General-purpose workstations matched specialized LISP-machine performance at lower cost. The LISP-hardware market collapsed, taking much of the expert-systems industry with it.

fieldChange.before: Specialized Lisp machines were the machines on which U.S. expert-systems work was expected to run.
fieldChange.after: A Symbolics history in an MIT course records a 1987 crisis: product revenue fell from $101.6 million in 1986 to $82.1 million in 1987 and $55.6 million in 1988, as general workstations became usable for Lisp.

exhibits.title: Google Photos gorilla mislabel
exhibits.publicStory: Google Photos labeled Black users as gorillas. Reporting describes a later fix that removed the word gorilla from the label set rather than retraining the model.

fieldChange.before: A wrong photo label was treated as a mistake a retrained model would simply stop making.
fieldChange.after: The incident report records the gorilla label. Gigazine describes a later fix that removed the word from the label set rather than retraining the model.

exhibits.title: Transformer citation-count claim
exhibits.publicStory: On 4 October 2026 the secondary page previously cited for a most-cited ranking did not answer, and no citation index was opened. This plaque does not state a rank.
exhibits.editorialNote: The Jerry Cards page returned 403 and was removed. No citation index was opened. The rank is not stated. Not canon.

fieldChange.before: A ranking of the Transformer paper among the most-cited papers of the century was carried from a single secondary page.
fieldChange.after: That page did not answer. The arXiv record is the paper itself, not a citation count, so the museum states no rank.

exhibits.title: 2025 winter-or-bubble debate
exhibits.publicStory: Commentary in 2025 explicitly compared the investment climate to the overpromise pattern of 1974 and 1987. The museum records this as an open debate.
exhibits.editorialNote: Disputed. Forbes returned 403 and is not cited. One 2025 commentary makes the comparison. The Wikipedia history records the earlier winters and does not itself declare a 2025 winter.

fieldChange.before: The downturns of 1974 and 1987 were history, and a 2025 comparison had not been filed on this wall.
fieldChange.after: One 2025 commentary compares the investment climate to those years. The Wikipedia history of AI winters records the earlier periods. Neither page is a finding that a new winter has begun.

exhibits.title: September 2026 frontier model names
exhibits.publicStory: OpenAI's own page, dated 9 July 2026, presents the GPT-5.6 family. Anthropic's own page presents Claude Opus 5.5. Names that appear only on aggregator sites are not listed.
exhibits.editorialNote: Perishable. Not canon. Names and dates in this node are expected to be wrong within weeks. Aggregator pages are not cited. GPT-6, Gemini, and Kimi were not on a lab page opened for this edit, so they are omitted.

fieldChange.before: A September 2026 aggregator list named models this museum had not opened on the labs' own pages.
fieldChange.after: The pages opened on 4 October 2026 are OpenAI's account of GPT-5.6 and Anthropic's account of Claude Opus 5.5.

claims.statement: The paper treats all-or-none neural events with propositional logic and defines nets whose behavior matches logical expressions.
For a logical expression meeting the paper's conditions, the calculus provides a net that behaves as that expression describes.
Nets that contain circles need more complicated logical means than the description used for nets without circles.
A technical failure is not established by the publisher abstract opened for this exhibit.
The publisher abstract says applications of the calculus are discussed. It does not name a remaining open problem.

The opened text says a finite set of equally likely messages can be measured by a logarithm of the number of messages.
The opened text sets semantic aspects of a message aside and treats the engineering problem as reproducing a selected message.

sources.title: A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity
sources.authors: Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts

blob.title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine
blob.publicStory: Menabrea's sketch of Babbage's Analytical Engine, translated with notes by Ada Lovelace, appeared in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs in 1843. Note G works through a table for the Bernoulli numbers.
blob.editorialNote: Gutenberg and the Wikisource sketch page are transcriptions. The Internet Archive item is a scan of Scientific Memoirs volume III (1843), where the sketch begins on page 666 and Note G gives the Bernoulli table. The separate Wikisource Notes subpage returned 404, so it is not cited.

figure.alt: Note G diagram titled Diagram for the computation by the Engine of the Numbers of Bernoulli.
figure.credit: Public-domain scan of the Bernoulli diagram. Wikimedia Commons file page states Public Domain Mark 1.0.

fieldChange.before: A calculating engine was discussed as a machine for tables, without a published general procedure written for it.
fieldChange.after: The 1843 translation of Menabrea's sketch, with Lovelace's Note G, works through a table for the Bernoulli numbers on the Analytical Engine.

blob.title: The Laws of Thought
blob.publicStory: The opened title page reads An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, on which are founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probabilities, by George Boole, London: Walton and Maberly, Cambridge: Macmillan and Co., 1854.
blob.editorialNote: The shipped scan is Internet Archive item aninvestigation00boolgoog, whose metadata says not in copyright in the US.

figure.alt: Title page reading An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, by George Boole, London, Walton and Maberly, 1854.
figure.credit: Title page of the 1854 edition. Public-domain scan from the Internet Archive.

fieldChange.before: Logic was taught as a verbal art, apart from the manipulation of algebraic equations.
fieldChange.after: The opened 1854 title page presents Boole's book as an investigation of the laws of thought on which the mathematical theories of logic and probabilities are founded.

blob.title: On Computable Numbers
blob.publicStory: A. M. Turing's On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem, appeared in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, series 2, volume 42.
blob.editorialNote: The opened Crossref record dates the print issue 1937. It does not give a received-in-1936 date. This room keeps 1936 as the working year.

figure.alt: A state table with rows q1 and q2 and columns for symbols 0 and 1.
figure.credit: Original state-table diagram, redrawn after the London Mathematical Society paper. The opened record dates the print issue 1937. Not a scan.

fieldChange.before: The Entscheidungsproblem asked whether a definite method could decide every statement of a formal system, without a published account of what such a method was.
fieldChange.after: Turing's paper in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society defines computable numbers by a machine and applies that definition to the Entscheidungsproblem.

blob.title: Relay and switching circuits
blob.publicStory: Claude Shannon's A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits appeared in the Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, volume 57, pages 713–723, in 1938.
blob.editorialNote: The DOI record was opened. The IEEE Xplore HTML was a bot challenge and was not read.

figure.alt: Two relay boxes in series with a lamp.
figure.credit: Original relay diagram for this room. Not a copy of a figure from the 1938 paper.

fieldChange.before: Relay circuits were drawn as electrical arrangements, and symbolic logic was a separate study.
fieldChange.after: Shannon's 1938 paper gives a symbolic analysis of relay and switching circuits, in the Transactions of the AIEE, volume 57, pages 713–723.

blob.title: McCulloch–Pitts neuron
blob.publicStory: McCulloch and Pitts published a calculus that treats all-or-none neural events with propositional logic and pairs logical expressions with nets.

figure.alt: Two input circles joined by lines to one output circle.
figure.credit: Original net diagram, redrawn after the 1943 paper. Not a copy of a journal figure.

blob.technicalAccount: The 1943 paper in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics states that the all-or-none character of nervous activity lets neural events be treated by propositional logic. A net without circles has a description in that logic, and a logical expression meeting their conditions has a net that behaves as the expression describes. Nets with circles need further logical means.

fieldChange.before: A neuron was described physiologically, and propositional logic was a separate calculus.
fieldChange.after: The 1943 paper treats all-or-none neural events with propositional logic and pairs a logical expression with a net that behaves as that expression describes.

blob.title: Cybernetics
blob.publicStory: A 1948 edition is catalogued as Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics; or, Control and communication in the animal and the machine, from The Technology Press. The Internet Archive scan cited here is the 1961 second edition from MIT Press, not the 1948 printing.
blob.editorialNote: Open Library's edition record was opened. A title page was not. The record does not name Hermann et Cie.

figure.alt: A box labeled effector with a return path from its output back to its input.
figure.credit: Original feedback diagram for this room. The catalog record has no figure to copy.

fieldChange.before: Control in machines and communication in animals were catalogued as separate subjects.
fieldChange.after: A 1948 edition is catalogued as Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics; or, Control and communication in the animal and the machine.

blob.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
blob.publicStory: Shannon's 1948 paper defines a communication system as information source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, and measures a choice among messages with a logarithm.

figure.alt: Five boxes in a row, labeled source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, with a noise mark above the channel.
figure.credit: Original diagram of the five parts named in the paper's text. Not a copy of the printed figure.

blob.technicalAccount: The paper's text names five parts of a communication system: information source, transmitter, channel, receiver, and destination, and it places a noise source on the channel. A message is one selected from a set of possible messages. When that set is finite and choices are equally likely, the measure is a logarithm of the number of messages. The discrete noiseless case is developed before the continuous case.

fieldChange.before: Communication engineering had no shared measure for a choice among possible messages.
fieldChange.after: The 1948 paper names an information source, a transmitter, a channel, a receiver, and a destination, and it measures a finite set of equally likely messages by a logarithm of that number.

blob.title: Turing's imitation game
blob.publicStory: Alan Turing published Computing Machinery and Intelligence in Mind, proposing the Imitation Game as an operational stand-in for whether machines can think.

fieldChange.before: Asking whether a machine can think had no agreed operation that would settle the question.
fieldChange.after: Turing's 1950 paper in Mind proposes the imitation game as a stand-in for that question.

blob.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
blob.publicStory: A summer workshop at Dartmouth, proposed in August 1955 as a “2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence”; the proposal's title introduced the term. It is widely regarded as the field's founding event.

fieldChange.before: Research on machines and intelligence had no common name.
fieldChange.after: The 31 August 1955 proposal, A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, asks for a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence.

blob.title: Rosenblatt's Perceptron
blob.publicStory: Frank Rosenblatt published the Perceptron, a probabilistic model of a learning network.

fieldChange.before: A learning machine was a proposal, not a published model with a training rule.
fieldChange.after: Rosenblatt's 1958 paper presents the perceptron as a probabilistic model for storing and organizing information.

blob.title: DENDRAL
blob.publicStory: The DENDRAL project at Stanford identified chemical structures. Its builders' 1993 case study calls it the first expert system for scientific hypothesis formation.

fieldChange.before: A program that proposed a chemical structure from instrument data was a hope, not a recorded project.
fieldChange.after: The builders' 1993 case study calls DENDRAL the first expert system for scientific hypothesis formation. The Computer History Museum keeps the project's papers.

blob.title: ELIZA
blob.publicStory: Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA, a pattern-matching conversational program. Many users treated it as understanding them, a documented case of over-attribution later called the Eliza effect.

fieldChange.before: A program that answered in sentences was easy to treat as a program that understood the person typing.
fieldChange.after: Weizenbaum's 1966 paper describes ELIZA as keyword rules that transform a sentence, and he writes that the relation of appearance to reality stays with the playwright.

blob.title: ALPAC report
blob.publicStory: The Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee report found machine translation had not delivered, after which U.S. government MT funding was sharply reduced.

fieldChange.before: U.S. agencies were funding machine translation in the expectation of a working system.
fieldChange.after: The 1966 National Academies report, Language and Machines, is the committee's published finding that machine translation had not delivered what that funding assumed.

blob.title: Limits of the single-layer perceptron
blob.publicStory: Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons proved formal limits of single-layer networks, including XOR.
blob.editorialNote: The MIT Press DOI is the 2017 reissue of the book; its page returned 403 and was not read. Open Library catalogues the 1969 printing. The XOR limit is also stated on the Wikipedia book page.

fieldChange.before: A single layer of neuron-like units was treated as a route to any classification that mattered.
fieldChange.after: Minsky and Papert's book, cited here in the MIT Press 2017 reissue, states formal limits of a single-layer perceptron, including exclusive-or. Open Library catalogues the 1969 printing.

blob.title: Lighthill Report
blob.publicStory: The Lighthill Report to the UK Science Research Council concluded AI had failed to produce the promised major impact, and was followed by deep UK funding cuts.
blob.editorialNote: The report is dated July 1972 and was published in 1973. The funding cuts that followed are stated on the Wikipedia page, not in the report.

fieldChange.before: UK support for artificial intelligence assumed the work would produce the impact that had been promised.
fieldChange.after: Lighthill's survey, in the Edinburgh copy, says that in no part of the field had the discoveries produced the major impact that was then promised. The Chilton host did not answer, so it is not cited.

blob.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
blob.publicStory: IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov.

fieldChange.before: No chess computer had beaten a reigning world champion in a match under regular time controls.
fieldChange.after: IBM's history says Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997, after Kasparov had won their 1996 match.

blob.title: Watson wins Jeopardy!
blob.publicStory: IBM Watson won Jeopardy! against the champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings in February 2011.

fieldChange.before: A question-answering system had not beaten the strongest human champions of a televised quiz on the air.
fieldChange.after: IBM's history says Watson defeated Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings on Jeopardy! in February 2011.

blob.title: AlexNet at ILSVRC
blob.publicStory: AlexNet won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a GPU-trained convolutional network, with a top-5 error rate of 15.3 percent, against 26.2 percent for the second-best entry.

fieldChange.before: The next-best ImageNet entry in 2012 still relied on engineered features, with a top-5 error of 26.2 percent.
fieldChange.after: The NeurIPS 2012 paper reports that an average of convolutional networks reached 15.3 percent top-5 error on ILSVRC-2012.

blob.title: Generative adversarial networks
blob.publicStory: Goodfellow and colleagues introduced generative adversarial networks.

fieldChange.before: A generator of new samples was trained to match a data set, without a second network trained to tell real from generated.
fieldChange.after: The 2014 paper proposes two models trained together: a generator, and a discriminator that estimates whether a sample came from the training data.

blob.title: Tay
blob.publicStory: Microsoft took its Tay chatbot offline within a day of its March 2016 Twitter launch, after Tay posted what Microsoft called wildly inappropriate and reprehensible words and images.

fieldChange.before: A public chatbot was launched on the assumption that conversation on the open internet would stay inside the filters shipped with it.
fieldChange.after: Microsoft's 25 March 2016 post is the team's account of taking Tay offline. The incident report dates the offensive posts to about 16 hours after the Twitter launch.

blob.title: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
blob.publicStory: DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Go player Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul in March 2016. In game two it played Move 37, which DeepMind's account says upended centuries of traditional wisdom.

fieldChange.before: A published Go program had not yet played a match against a player of Lee Sedol's standing.
fieldChange.after: Nature's January 2016 paper is the account of the network-and-search program. DeepMind's own page is the record of the later match: a 4–1 win over Lee Sedol in Seoul in March 2016.

blob.title: Attention Is All You Need
blob.publicStory: Eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research (one listed at the University of Toronto, with work performed at Google) published Attention Is All You Need, introducing the Transformer. The paper reports 28.4 BLEU on WMT-2014 English–German and 41.8 BLEU on English–French after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs. Authors are credited as equal contributors.

fieldChange.before: The strongest translation models were recurrent or convolutional networks, with attention as a connection between an encoder and a decoder.
fieldChange.after: The paper proposes a network that uses attention alone, and it reports 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French after 3.5 days on eight GPUs.

blob.title: AlphaFold2
blob.publicStory: DeepMind's AlphaFold2 made highly accurate protein-structure prediction from amino-acid sequence possible, a long-standing structural-biology challenge.

fieldChange.before: A protein's folded shape was predicted from its sequence only approximately, and the hard targets at the structure contest were still mostly unsolved.
fieldChange.after: The result shown at CASP14 in 2020 was published in Nature in 2021. The paper reports highly accurate structure prediction from amino-acid sequence. The plaque keeps 2020 as the year of that contest.

blob.title: ChatGPT research preview
blob.publicStory: OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free research preview on 30 November 2022.
blob.editorialNote: The 100 million users clause was removed. No news page stating that figure was opened. The OpenAI post is the 30 November 2022 announcement.

fieldChange.before: A large language model was available through an API and demos, not as a free conversational research preview.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's 30 November 2022 post introduces ChatGPT as a free research preview, trained to answer in dialogue.

blob.title: Statement on AI Risk
blob.publicStory: The Center for AI Safety's one-sentence statement on extinction-scale AI risk was signed by AI researchers and the heads of major labs. A survey of AI-conference authors, published in January 2024, found that between 38 and 51 percent of respondents gave at least a 10 percent chance to advanced AI leading to outcomes as bad as human extinction. That range is a survey statistic, not a consensus forecast.

fieldChange.before: Extinction-scale risk from AI was a topic of talks, without one short public statement from lab leaders and without a counted survey of conference authors.
fieldChange.after: The Center for AI Safety published a one-sentence statement on that risk. The survey paper, published in January 2024, says between 38 and 51 percent of respondents gave at least a 10 percent chance to advanced AI leading to outcomes as bad as human extinction.

blob.title: EU AI Act
blob.publicStory: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on 1 August 2024 as a horizontal AI law with a phased, risk-tiered timeline. The regulation sets fines of up to €35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of the Article 5 prohibitions.

fieldChange.before: Rules for AI systems in the European Union were national or sectoral, without one horizontal regulation in force.
fieldChange.after: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on EUR-Lex, sets a fine of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5. The plaque dates entry into force, not a later consolidated text.

blob.title: 2024 Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry
blob.publicStory: The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for work enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded half to David Baker for computational protein design, and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction.

fieldChange.before: The physics and chemistry prizes had not been given for the machine-learning work named here.
fieldChange.after: The Nobel Foundation's 2024 summaries award physics to John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for discoveries that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks, and chemistry half to David Baker for computational protein design and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences says Hassabis and Jumper developed AlphaFold2.

blob.title: BERT
blob.publicStory: Google's BERT pre-trained a Transformer on plain text, reading the words on both sides of each gap, then fine-tuned it to new state-of-the-art results on eleven language tasks. Google open-sourced it in November 2018, saying anyone could train a state-of-the-art question-answering system in about 30 minutes on a single Cloud TPU.

fieldChange.before: Pre-trained language models read text in one direction, or joined a left-to-right model with a right-to-left one.
fieldChange.after: The 2018 paper pre-trains a Transformer on the words to both sides at once, and reports new state-of-the-art results on eleven language tasks after fine-tuning.

blob.title: GPT-2
blob.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-2, a 1.5-billion-parameter Transformer trained on millions of web pages, set state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language-modelling datasets without being trained for any of them. OpenAI released it in stages.
blob.editorialNote: Both sources are OpenAI's own; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains. The paper PDF is undated: 2019 rests on the GitHub repository and the Epoch AI date of 14 February 2019.

fieldChange.before: Language tasks were approached by training a model on a labelled data set for each task.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's paper reports that a 1.5-billion-parameter model trained on WebText, a data set of millions of web pages, set state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language-modelling data sets without training on them.

blob.title: GPT-3
blob.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, which its paper calls 10 times more than any previous non-sparse language model. It performed many tasks from a few examples written as text, with no fine-tuning.

fieldChange.before: A language model needed a fine-tuning data set of thousands of labelled examples for each new task.
fieldChange.after: The 2020 paper reports that GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, performed many tasks from a few examples given as text, with no fine-tuning.

blob.title: Wu Dao 2.0
blob.publicStory: Wu Dao 2.0, with 1.75 trillion parameters, was released in June 2021, and its creators say that is ten times as many as GPT-3. Tsinghua University says it understands and generates text and images in Chinese, English and other mainstream languages, and that its development was led by Jie Tang, a Tsinghua professor and vice director of academics at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence.
blob.editorialNote: No page from the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence was found, so the story says only what Tsinghua's page says. That page is undated and says the model was released in June; Engadget's report of 2 June 2021 dates the year.

fieldChange.before: China's first super-scale natural-language model had been unveiled in early 2021.
fieldChange.after: Tsinghua's account says Wu Dao 2.0 was released in June with 1.75 trillion parameters, which its creators put at ten times GPT-3.

blob.title: Chinchilla
blob.publicStory: DeepMind found that large language models were undertrained, and that model size and training data should grow together. Its 70-billion-parameter Chinchilla used the same compute as the 280-billion-parameter Gopher with four times the data, and outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 and Megatron-Turing NLG on a large range of tasks.

fieldChange.before: Language models were being scaled up in size while the amount of training data stayed about the same.
fieldChange.after: The 2022 paper finds that model size and training tokens should be scaled equally. Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and four times Gopher's data for the same compute, outperforms Gopher.

blob.title: LLaMA
blob.publicStory: Meta released LLaMA in February 2023 in four sizes from 7 to 65 billion parameters, trained only on publicly available data, under a noncommercial research licence. Its paper reports that the 13-billion-parameter version outperforms the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

fieldChange.before: The strongest language models were trained in part on data sets that were not publicly available.
fieldChange.after: The 2023 paper trains models from 7 to 65 billion parameters on publicly available data alone, and reports that the 13-billion-parameter model outperforms GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

blob.title: GPT-4
blob.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-4 accepts images and text and produces text, and its technical report says it passed a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers. The report also says OpenAI predicted parts of GPT-4's performance from models trained with no more than 1/1,000th of its compute.
blob.editorialNote: Both sources carry OpenAI's own document; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains.

fieldChange.before: OpenAI's earlier GPT-3.5 scored around the bottom 10% of test takers on a simulated bar exam.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's 2023 technical report says GPT-4, which accepts images and text, passed the simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers.

blob.title: Qwen
blob.publicStory: Alibaba Cloud released its Qwen language models openly on ModelScope and Hugging Face, starting with Qwen-7B on 3 August 2023. The series grew to base and chat models of 1.8, 7, 14 and 72 billion parameters.

fieldChange.before: Alibaba Cloud had not released the weights of its Qwen language models.
fieldChange.after: The QwenLM repository records the open release of Qwen-7B on ModelScope and Hugging Face on 3 August 2023, and base and chat models of 1.8, 7, 14 and 72 billion parameters.

blob.title: Falcon-180B
blob.publicStory: The Technology Innovation Institute's Falcon-180B has 180 billion parameters and was trained on over 3.5 trillion tokens, which its authors call the largest openly documented pretraining run. TII released it under a permissive licence, alongside 7B and 40B models.
blob.editorialNote: The model card gives no release date. The paper is from November 2023 and Epoch AI gives 6 September 2023.

fieldChange.before: No openly documented language-model pretraining run had used 3.5 trillion tokens.
fieldChange.after: The Falcon paper says Falcon-180B was trained on over 3.5 trillion tokens, the largest openly documented pretraining run. TII released it with 7B and 40B models under a permissive licence.

blob.title: Mistral 7B
blob.publicStory: Mistral AI, a French company headquartered in Paris, released Mistral 7B, a 7.3-billion-parameter model, on 27 September 2023 under the Apache 2.0 licence, so anyone could use it without restrictions. The company says it outperforms Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks.
blob.editorialNote: Neither Mistral source states the country; the Wikipedia article says the company is French and headquartered in Paris.

fieldChange.before: Llama 2 13B, with almost twice the parameters, was the open model Mistral 7B was measured against.
fieldChange.after: Mistral AI's 27 September 2023 announcement releases the 7.3-billion-parameter Mistral 7B under Apache 2.0 and says it outperforms Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks.

blob.title: OpenAI o1
blob.publicStory: OpenAI's o1 models are trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using a chain of thought, so they can produce a long chain of thought before they answer. OpenAI's system card, dated 5 December 2024, says o1 was previously called o1-preview.
blob.editorialNote: Both sources carry OpenAI's own document; the owner accepted the two OpenAI domains. The arXiv copy was revised later; the story uses the original date.

fieldChange.before: OpenAI's chat models were not trained to produce a long chain of thought before answering.
fieldChange.after: OpenAI's o1 system card, dated 5 December 2024, says the o1 models are trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought.

blob.title: DeepSeek-V3
blob.publicStory: DeepSeek-V3 is a mixture-of-experts model with 671 billion parameters, of which 37 billion are active for each token, pre-trained on 14.8 trillion tokens. Its report says full training took 2.788 million H800 GPU hours, and DeepSeek released the weights with commercial use allowed.

fieldChange.before: A dense language model uses all of its parameters for every token.
fieldChange.after: The DeepSeek-V3 report describes a mixture-of-experts model with 671 billion parameters, 37 billion active for each token, whose full training took 2.788 million H800 GPU hours.

blob.title: DeepSeek-R1
blob.publicStory: DeepSeek showed that a language model's reasoning could be improved through reinforcement learning alone, without human-written reasoning examples, and published the work in Nature in September 2025. DeepSeek released R1's weights under the MIT licence and says R1 performs comparably to OpenAI's o1 on maths, code and reasoning.
blob.editorialNote: Nature 645, 633–638 (2025). The arXiv copy was revised later; the story uses the original dates.

fieldChange.before: Reasoning in language models was improved by training on human-written reasoning examples.
fieldChange.after: The Nature paper reports that R1's reasoning was improved through reinforcement learning alone, without human-labelled reasoning examples.

blob.title: GPT-6 Astra
blob.publicStory: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra system card (3 September 2026) calls it the most capable model OpenAI has ever broadly deployed, and the first to reach the Critical level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework. Constellation Research reported that OpenAI launched it first to customers in its Daybreak program, before broad availability.
blob.editorialNote: The plaque states no hardware or GPU count: OpenAI's pages that could be opened do not name the hardware. Training compute is an Epoch AI estimate and appears only on the Globe.

fieldChange.before: No model OpenAI had deployed had reached the Critical level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework.
fieldChange.after: The 3 September 2026 system card says GPT-6 Astra is the first to reach that level. Constellation Research reports the same, calling Astra OpenAI's first launch with critical cybersecurity capability.

blob.title: Mechanical and logical precursors
blob.publicStory: Nilsson's history treats Aristotle's syllogism as important for its form, Boole's 1854 Laws of Thought as showing that some logical reasoning can be done by manipulating equations, and Babbage's engines as engineering clues in that quest.
blob.editorialNote: Framing plaque. Nilsson's pages say the print version is Cambridge University Press and ask readers not to cite this PDF. The URL is the file that was opened. Not a single technical result.

figure.credit: Original illustration of the years in this room. Not a plate from Nilsson.

fieldChange.before: A history of the field could open at the first meeting that used the name, and leave earlier logic and machinery outside it.
fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey places the form of the syllogism, Boole's 1854 equations, and Babbage's engines inside that history, as clues rather than as one technical result.

blob.title: Mechanical and logical precursors
blob.publicStory: Nilsson's history treats Aristotle's syllogism as important for its form, Boole's 1854 Laws of Thought as showing that some logical reasoning can be done by manipulating equations, and Babbage's engines as engineering clues in that quest.
blob.editorialNote: Framing plaque. Nilsson's pages say the print version is Cambridge University Press and ask readers not to cite this PDF. The URL is the file that was opened. Not a single technical result.

fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey places the form of the syllogism, Boole's 1854 equations, and Babbage's engines inside that history, as clues rather than as one technical result.

blob.title: First AI winter
blob.publicStory: Retrospectives treat 1974–1980 as the first AI winter, when inflated promises met computational and theoretical limits of symbolic AI.

fieldChange.before: The funding cuts after 1973 were separate decisions, not yet one named period.
fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey is one later history that places those years in a longer story. The name AI winter is the label on the Wikipedia page for 1974–1980, not a name from 1974 itself.

blob.title: First AI winter
blob.publicStory: Retrospectives treat 1974–1980 as the first AI winter, when inflated promises met computational and theoretical limits of symbolic AI.

fieldChange.before: The funding cuts after 1973 were separate decisions, not yet one named period.
fieldChange.after: Nilsson's survey is one later history that places those years in a longer story. The name AI winter is the label on the Wikipedia page for 1974–1980, not a name from 1974 itself.

versions.reason: Withdrawn: A later label for a period, not a documented event. Both sources were secondary histories.

blob.title: Expert systems commercial boom
blob.publicStory: A 1985 government report estimated AI-related activity funded by government and industry at about $400 million that year. A separate 1985 note put sales of AI software and hardware at about $150 million a year.
blob.editorialNote: The billion-dollar sentence was not on an institutional page opened for this edit. The $400 million estimate is the 1985 Argonne report. The $150 million sales figure is a 1985 journal note.

fieldChange.before: Expert systems were laboratory programs, without a published government estimate of that year's spending.

blob.title: LISP-machine market collapse
blob.publicStory: General-purpose workstations matched specialized LISP-machine performance at lower cost. The LISP-hardware market collapsed, taking much of the expert-systems industry with it.
